articles.title_orig: Wartime memory shows the China-Russia partnership is anything but ‘limitless’
articles.title_zh: Wartime memory shows the China-Russia partnership is anything but ‘limitless’
articles.content_orig:
For more than a decade, China and Russia have sought to align their official memories of the second world war. They have staged prominent joint commemorations and military parades, while also coordinating remembrance dates and harmonising their official discourses about the war.
The latest example of this “memory alliance” came in September when the Chinese and Russian ambassadors to New Zealand, Wang Xiaolong and Stanislav Krans, published a joint opinion article in the NZ Herald to mark the 81st anniversary of the war’s end.
Their article insisted the lessons of the war must not be forgotten. They said this entails safeguarding the UN‑centred international order and rejecting historical revisionism that downplays Chinese and Russian sacrifices or glosses over Nazi and fascist atrocities.
China and Russia’s memory alliance serves two main purposes. First, it deepens the supposedly “limitless” partnership between the two countries. Second, it forms the basis for them to defend what they regard as the foundations of the post‑war global order.
In their view, the core principles of the global order that emerged from the second world war are multilateralism, sovereignty and non‑interference in other countries’ internal affairs. They claim these hard-won gains are being undermined by what they portray as US‑led western arrogance, aggression and unilateralism.
For Beijing, this perceived subversion has taken the form of semiconductor export bans, tariffs on Chinese EVs, efforts to contain China’s influence in the Indo-Pacific and Japan’s growing military role in the region. China also views western support for Taiwan, which reverted to Chinese control after Japan’s defeat in 1945, as a violation of the post-war order.
For Moscow, the threat comes from Nato’s enlargement, perceived western interference in Ukraine culminating in President Viktor Yanukovych’s ousting in 2014 and the global sanctions regime imposed after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russian leaders accuse the west of disregarding Russia’s “legitimate interests” and security concerns.
Invoking the “scourge” of the second world war enables both Russia and China to frame these concerns while advocating a multipolar world defined by regional spheres of influence. Yet, as my research shows , three trends in Russia and China’s official war remembrance reveal strains in their proclaimed no-limits partnership .
First, there is little convergence in their historical narratives on key episodes of the war or on the nature of their wartime relationship. Both sides advance different claims about who contributed most to defeating Japan and who assisted whom.
Russian narratives emphasise the Red Army’s decisive contribution, downplaying China’s role in tying down Japanese forces. Beijing, meanwhile, suggests it made the largest sacrifice among the allies. It claims to have been decisive in prolonging Japan’s entanglement in China and securing its ultimate defeat.
In 2023, I carried out an analysis of more than 14,000 Chinese and Russian state-sponsored news articles with my colleague Eric Zhang. Combined with extensive fieldwork in China, our findings suggest that convergence with Russia’s preferred historical narratives has been limited to shared silences about episodes that would embarrass each other.
These include wartime mutual frictions or Soviet crimes during the liberation of north-eastern China.
Even more striking, given the strategic importance both sides attach to their friendship, is how little they have made of personal wartime stories. This is despite the rich historical material available for constructing a shared memory.
Roughly 1,500 Soviet advisers and 2,000 combat pilots supported China’s early war effort. About 200 of these so-called “Flying Eagles” were killed. Yet their stories remain largely unknown to the public, with only a few of these aviators commemorated in China.
One exception is Hryhorij Kulishenko, a Ukrainian-born Soviet Air Force pilot who was killed during the battle for Wuhan in October 1939. During a 2013 state visit to Russia, Chinese leader Xi Jinping highlighted Kulishenko’s story as a symbol of enduring solidarity between the two countries.
Addressing the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, Xi described Kulishenko as a hero who had fought “side by side with the Chinese people” and would never be forgotten. But in recent years, these “Flying Eagles” have gradually faded from China’s official narrative of friendship with Russia.
By contrast, Chinese official accounts and history exhibitions are replete with references to Sino‑US cooperation during the war, especially the American volunteer group of the Chinese Air Force known as the “Flying Tigers”. They have been portrayed by Chinese state media as a lasting symbol of shared struggle and friendship.
This leads to the second trend: the China-Russia memory alliance is being diluted by Beijing’s increasingly active memory diplomacy toward the US.
China’s efforts to highlight its wartime cooperation with the US reached a peak during Xi’s recent state visit to Washington. At the White House welcome ceremony, Donald Trump echoed Xi’s praise for the Flying Tigers. He even recalled that the US and China had fought together as “allies” during the war.
The third trend is the recent emergence of Ukraine in China’s second world war commemorations.
In September 2025, on the 80th anniversary of Victory Day, the Chinese embassy in Kyiv donated a bronze statue of Kulishenko – the very pilot Xi had praised in Moscow in 2013 as a symbol of China-Russia friendship – to a memorial in Cherepyn, his birthplace.
This gesture reflects a subtle but significant shift in how China frames the memory of this celebrated Soviet hero , moving from his earlier mobilisation for Chinese-Russian friendship towards a Sino‑Ukrainian narrative.
In China, official war memory is closely tied to policy direction. After more than a decade of cultivating a “no‑limits” friendship with Moscow, this latest adjustment of wartime remembrance may reveal Beijing’s unease with being perceived as aligned too closely with Russia.
Partnering with Russia may help Beijing selectively uphold and revive certain elements of the post‑war global order. But China is simultaneously signalling that it seeks continued cooperation with the west and does not wish to become alienated or isolated.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic eyes $1.4 trillion IPO valuation in test of Wall Street's AI fervor
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic eyes $1.4 trillion IPO valuation in test of Wall Street's AI fervor
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, according to an updated filing on Tuesday, bringing the 5-year-old artificial intelligence lab a step closer to a potentially historic Nasdaq debut.
The company is planning to price on Nov. 18 and trade on Nov. 19, according to people familiar with the details who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is targeting retail allocation of about 20%, the people said, a much higher percentage than the typical initial public offering, which is 5% to 10% for retail investors.
At the high end of the range, Anthropic would net up to $64.35 billion in proceeds through the IPO. The company could end up being worth up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, rising from the $965 billion valuation it announced as part of a funding round in May.
Anthropic said it has entered into an agreement with Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. to purchase $26 billion of the company's Class N common stock in a private placement at a price per share equal to the IPO price. The shares sold in the private placement will not be registered in the offering and will not be subject to lock-up agreements with the underwriters, the company said.
As Anthropic executives get set to pitch the offering to investors, they have to contend with a tumultuous political environment , following last week's midterm elections that included a Democratic sweep in Congress and the passage of numerous statewide ballot measures that could slow the AI buildout. They're also facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade on concern that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases.
CNBC reported last week that some Anthropic investors were bracing for a lower valuation than had previously been expected. While Anthropic had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation until recently, shareholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a "stretch."
Should Anthropic reach the Nasdaq this month as planned, under the ticker symbol "ANT," the debut would come roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. Elon Musk's reusable rocket and AI company has a market cap of just under $2 trillion, around its valuation at the time of the IPO.
Institutional demand for Anthropic is even stronger than it was for SpaceX at this point in the process, the people said. The company's book is already covered at the $70 to $78 per share range on an allocable basis, they said.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the AI lab in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and the company primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
On Monday, Anthropic introduced two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the first time the company has released so-called frontier models since Amodei called to slow down the pace of AI development in September . Anthropic said that the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing, and that the company developed new evaluations and post-launch monitoring tools ahead of the release.
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic said in its amended filing Tuesday that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.
"Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort. We hope you will share our ambition to see it though."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy could be a problem for the economy
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy could be a problem for the economy
articles.content_orig:
Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., said on a Tuesday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" that Congress needs to "get to the bottom" of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Moolenaar, who chairs the House Permanent Select Committee on China, said he wants to know whether Huang shared privileged information with a Chinese spy; whether Huang was influenced to lobby against preventing chip sales to China; and whether China was given preference in purchasing Nvidia's limited supply of advanced chips.
And he urged a thorough internal investigation of Huang.
"If it becomes less of an investigation, more of damage control, that's not going to work because people have to have confidence," Moolenaar said.
"We're dealing with the country, the Chinese Communist Party that is a foremost adversary, that's funding wars and supporting Russia, supporting Iran, North Korea," he said. "And we have basically a Cold War race with technology. We cannot allow the premier company at the forefront of this to, in some way, be irresponsible."
Congressional scrutiny of Huang's affair has intensified since members returned to Washington on Monday.
The New York Times reported that Huang was romantically involved with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who U.S. intelligence agencies have identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia opened an investigation into its CEO on Sunday. The two Huangs are not related.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , D-N.Y., said in a press conference on Monday that "we're going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of national security"
Moolenaar co-authored a letter with Florida Rep. Brian Mast and Arkansas Rep. Rick Crawford on Nov. 5 asking Huang to appear before the Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Select Committee on Intelligence. Mast chairs the foreign affairs panel, and Crawford chairs intelligence.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the three Republicans wrote.

articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Opens Lower After Inflation Report — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion for its upcoming IPO, with the company looking to raise as much as $64.4bn in what would be one of the largest stock market debuts in history.
The company, which makes the Claude AI chatbot, launched its investor roadshow on Tuesday, with reported plans to go public next week.
According to its filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Tuesday, Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78, giving it a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion when potential shares are included.
It has also secured $26bn in a separate private placement backed by some of the world’s largest tech companies, including Google, Nvidia , Microsoft and AMD.
The listing is being closely watched as a major test for how much investors are still willing to bet on AI companies, which have driven huge gains in tech stocks and the broader US market.
The $1.4 trillion valuation is lower than earlier estimates, which had suggested Anthropic could be valued between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, as concerns grow about the company’s enormous infrastructure spending and recent swings in AI stock prices.
Those concerns extend beyond Anthropic, with investors increasingly questioning whether AI companies can make enough money to justify their soaring valuations and sustain the boom.
Despite the uncertainty, Anthropic’s growth has been explosive .
The company reported revenues of $17bn in their third quarter, up from $1.4bn a year earlier, as its net losses narrowed. On Tuesday, Anthropic said it was on pace to generate about $81bn in annual revenue, $10bn higher than its estimate a month earlier.
The company credits its growth to the demand for Claude, including from industries like healthcare, financial services and legal services.
But to keep up with that demand, Anthropic has committed almost $900bn to computing costs with partners including Amazon and Google, a massive financial bet on continued demand for its product.
The IPO also lands in an uncertain political climate, with Democrats having just won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections last week. The new Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate have raised the prospect of more regulation of AI companies and new restrictions on the construction of data centres that power the technology.
AI stocks slid after the midterms, with the Nasdaq falling 5.5 percent on Thursday, its biggest one-day drop in more than a year. The selloff, also driven by declines at Nvidia, whose CEO was targeted by an alleged Chinese spy , wiped out trillions of dollars from the market.
Markets have since recovered some of those losses, though the Nasdaq dipped slightly below 1 percent on Tuesday. Some analysts argued the sell-off was an overreaction and that the election was unlikely to derail the expansion of data centres.

articles.title_orig: Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.title_zh: Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.content_orig:
Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's foreign intelligence service (third from the right), speaks during the coordination meeting before the trilateral talks between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the U.S. in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, Tuesday. Altaf Qadri/Pool AP hide caption
ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Three-way talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates as Washington made another push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbor nearly five years ago.
Hopes of ending Europe's biggest conflict since World War II are tempered by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks earlier this year.
There's nothing to suggest a new posture that would lead to a breakthrough, but circumstances surrounding the talks have been changed by the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections as well as increased pressure on Russia's wartime economy. Moscow also is seeking to break Ukrainians' will as winter sets in by ramping up its battering of the country's power grid.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the nearly four-hour talks were "constructive and quite substantive," and largely were about humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country. Security guarantees also were discussed, he added during an appearance at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark.
Speaking in Paris at the Group of Seven meeting, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the talks were "very productive," but added: "There's a lot of work to be done in that regard."
The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February on the war, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians. A second round is expected Wednesday.
United Arab Emirates Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan sits flanked by Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law (left), and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff during talks between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the U.S. in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, Tuesday. Altaf Qadri/Pool AP hide caption
U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who along with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff is trying to broker a settlement, said he believed there were "some good ideas how to bridge" the differences between the two sides.
Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. elections. Democrats could demand more support for Ukraine.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told ZDF television on Monday night that "I don't have overly high expectations" for the talks.
There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks come against a backdrop of new long-range strikes by both Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.
Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces downed 155 Ukrainian drones overnight in eight Russian regions, as well as over the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014.
Kushner said in opening remarks that the goal of the talks is to "create a new framework and a new understanding building upon the different institutions and understandings of the past."
"We take what's worked, we try to identify what's failed, why we're in this position and hopefully create a new framework that leads us for decades, if not centuries, of peace," he said.
NATO commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who was also present, pointed to "some great progress in the past in a military-to-military dialogue in a trilateral format."
He said that the U.S. delegation looked forward "to working with both sides as we seek to advance the progress we've made in the past and continue this pursuit to set the foundations for a lasting peace."
Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service who leads Kyiv's delegation, thanked the U.S. for its efforts to end Russia's invasion.
"Our people are waiting to end this war. And we hope that we will achieve the lasting peace for Ukraine," he said.
The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, expressed hope the meeting "will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine."
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy walks alongside Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, right, as he arrives at the Danish Parliament Christiansborg, in Copenhagen, Tuesday. Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix via AP hide caption
Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.
The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal.
Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from four regions of Ukraine that Moscow annexed in September 2022 but has never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.
Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.
UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan speaks to U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff during the trilateral talks between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the US in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, Tuesday. Altaf Qadri/Pool AP hide caption
Zelenskyy rejects Putin's demands to voluntarily cede territory. He also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.
Ukraine argues an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled. Putin has spurned those suggestions.
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.
Russia's chief negotiator is Medinsky, a Putin aide who has led Moscow's team since the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff's operational department Yuri Zhigarlovsky.
Besides Umerov, the Ukrainian delegation also reportedly includes Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy, Sergiy Kyslytsya, and Davyd Arakhamia, the parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy's Servant of the People party.
Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as "a big agreement" that is "going to involve more than Ukraine."
Kushner said Monday on X that a "comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them."
Moscow has praised the broad approach.
"We can only welcome the (U.S.) negotiators on President Donald Trump's request proposing to put the issue of collective security on top of the agenda of the talks on a Ukrainian settlement," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
Some in the European Union see Washington's proposals as too accommodating to Moscow.
Russia has objected to the Europeans' involvement in the three-way talks, but said EU representatives could join at a later stage.

articles.title_orig: Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth
articles.title_zh: Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth
articles.content_orig:
Google’s Find Hub had a tumultuous launch for its performance , but also for a lack of clear direction in hardware. Over two years later, that’s finally arriving in the Google Pixel Tag which, even just a few days in, is the obvious gold standard in the race to build an AirTag for Android devices.
There are plenty of really good Android Find Hub trackers on the market. Pebblebee and Chipolo have been long-standing examples of how to build good dual-network trackers that work on both Android and iOS, while Motorola’s Moto Tag series has delivered two Android-only trackers that deliver better performance and more focused features. But even with the Moto Tag, there’s a clear compromise. Features like the ability to ring your phone are tied to a separate app and, in turn, have some inherent clunkiness.
Pixel Tag is the device that finally brings it all together, and it’s brilliant so far.
I’ve only had the Pixel Tag for a week and, frankly, it’s impossible to properly review a tracker in that time. There are only so many ways to artificially test out how a tracker works, as most cases where you’ll find value in this sort of product can only occur in real life.
So, with that said, let’s focus on the fundamentals.
Google Pixel Tag pairs to your Android phone just like any other Find Hub tracker – though much faster compared to some others I’ve tested – but the differences are obvious towards the end of that process. The final screen shows options for setting ringer volume and an option to set up “Ring this phone.”
Those new features are what make the Pixel Tag so good, and so appealing compared to all of the competition. A quick double-tap on the Tag’s button rings whichever phone you connected it to, assuming it’s in range, and it works pretty reliably. You can also set up “left behind” alerts (now available on other Find Hub trackers too) for when the phone leaves the tracker behind – you can set up exclusion zones such as your home or work address.
One of my favorite examples of the added polish from Google is the ability to adjust the ringer volume on the page where you actually want to ring the tracker. In a crowded but quiet space where you know the tracker is close by, being able to quickly set the volume to low is a great addition. In my book, it’s the reason to buy Pixel Tag over any other Android tracker.
UWB, of course, only makes up-close finding all the better. I found this decently reliable on my Pixel 11 Pro XL, but it is a little bit frustrating that the directional cues vanish within about 10-12 feet. Fine for a backpack or something like that, potentially a problem if your Tag is attached to a set of keys.
On that note, my biggest hardware complaint is that Google took the Apple route of having no built-in mounting mechanism. The super thin and light hardware of Pixel Tag is wonderful, don’t get me wrong, but being forced to buy a separate accessory just to attach it to my bag is frustrating! One of Google’s partners, Bellroy, built one of these accessories and it’s simple enough – a silicone case with a rope. I wish I didn’t need it, but it works, and at least you get two of them in a pack for $25.
The hardware itself is pretty good across the board, really, with the battery door also being slightly easier to open compared to the Moto Tag. Inside is a standard CR2032 battery that Google says will last “over one year.” I’d personally still prefer a rechargeable battery with USB-C or wireless charging, but this is a good enough solution given the amount of time the battery lasts – hopefully Google’s claim lives up.
Rounding out some of the key aspects here, it’s worth saying that the built-in speaker is more than loud enough at its highest setting, but the value for me so far has really come in that the low setting is actually low enough to not be a nuisance. I do find it a little strange that there’s no visual indication of where the Tag’s button is, but the packaging and app both do a good enough job of letting you know.
Overall performance in Find Hub seems fine, but as mentioned at the outset, this is a really hard thing to test artificially, all the more so in the span of just a few days. Google’s Find Hub network has gotten a lot better in the past two years, but it’s still hit or miss in my experience. It’s very clear that Google is making an effort to reverse the privacy-inspired decision to effectively disable the Find Hub network outside of crowded areas, but the damage has been done. I’m not sure the network will ever fully recover from that misstep, regardless of what tracker you’re using it with.
I’m looking forward to seeing how Pixel Tag performs as the travel season spins back up, so stay tuned for a later long-term review of Google’s tracker in the coming months. Initial impressions, though, are solid. Sound off in the comments below if you have any questions around Pixel Tag, I’ll answer everything I can!
If you’re interested in picking up a Pixel Tag, it’ll be available on November 11.

articles.title_orig: China extends rare earth and battery export control pause to 2027
articles.title_zh: China extends rare earth and battery export control pause to 2027
articles.content_orig:
China has extended its suspension of the export controls on rare earths, lithium ion batteries and graphite anode materials it announced in October 2025. The extension runs only until 10 January 2027. The original announcement suspended the restrictions for a year.

articles.title_orig: Stocks, Bonds Fall as CPI Data Fuel Fed-Hike Bets: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks, Bonds Fall as CPI Data Fuel Fed-Hike Bets: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Stocks fell on Tuesday after October inflation data came in hotter than expected and a key Federal Reserve official hinted at the possibility of a half-point rise in rates next month.
The S&P 500 traded down 0.9%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 302 points, or 0.6%. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.6%.
Nvidia dragged down the three major averages, falling 6%. The stock sat out Monday's tech-fueled rally following CEO Jensen Huang's admission over the weekend to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .
The consumer price index rose 0.4% in October, above the gain of 0.3% that economists polled by Dow Jones expected. Core CPI — which excludes volatile food and energy costs — increased 0.3% in October, whereas economists had called for a 0.2% advance. Annual figures were not be provided for Tuesday's report because of the 2025 government shutdown.
Treasury yields jumped as traders reacted to the report, fearing that interest rate increases could now be more likely in 2027. The 10-year Treasury note yield in particular advanced back above 5% .
Earlier Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in a speech in London that he thinks a December rate hike is likely and opened the door for a possible half-point increase amid persistent  inflationary pressures.
"While the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does," he said.
Traders now see a December rate hike as a near certainty and a small chance of a supersized increase. They also expect at least a quarter-point hike at some point next year.
"There's an extrapolation that maybe the Fed's going to have to hike rates more aggressively next year," said Tom Hainlin, national investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management. He later added, "The CPI print said perhaps inflation is going to be a little stickier for a little longer."
Tuesday's retreat came one day after the S&P 500 posted its best day since April. The push and pull come after a rocky week for markets, in which traders grew concerned about the potential for a slowdown in data center buildouts after Democrats posted big victories in the midterm elections.
Check out CNBC's live blog to read more about the stocks making midday moves here .
— John Melloy, Deena Zaidi and Darla Mercado
Nike is hosting its first Investor Day since 2017 next week under a new management team led by CEO Elliott Hill.
The event could serve as a crucial moment for the company that has been struggling to turn its business around.
"Next week will be an opportunity for management to signal the pathway ahead for Nike's medium-term growth story," Bernstein analyst Aneesha Sherman wrote in a Tuesday research note.
Investors are weighing up when the sportswear's business will stabilize from stagnating sales and lack of product innovation.
In the foreseeable future, analysts estimate Nike's five-year sales growth "will likely be flattish."
Bernstein sees Fiscal year 2027 as a "reset" in the Lifestyle category modeling a mid-teens decline, while Nike's other core segment, Performance grows 10%.
While the event itself may not be a catalyst for the stock which has gained 12% over the last month, Bernstein said it could "drive incremental investor confidence of a multi-year recovery."
The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped on Tuesday, moving back above the key 5% level, after hotter-than-expected inflation data .
The yield climbed more than 14 basis points to 5.004%. It last traded above the 5% level earlier this month. Read more .
Dallas Federal Reserve President Lorie Logan said Tuesday that she expects two more interest rate hikes will be needed as the central bank struggles to bring inflation lower.
"Tighter policy will be necessary to appropriately balance the outlook and risks for inflation and employment. And it is important to achieve that balance promptly," the policymaker said during an energy conference in Houston. "The longer above-target inflation persists, the greater the risk that it becomes baked into behavior."
Earlier in the day, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he expects a quarter percentage point hike would be appropriate at the next policy meeting in December. He even raised the notion that the Fed may have to raise by half a point should inflation numbers come in higher than expected, as they did in Tuesday's consumer price index report.
However, Logan said she thinks two more quarter-point moves would be appropriate before the Fed could take a break.
"The exact pace of increases could depend on the near-term economic and financial environment," she said. "After two more increases are in place, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate. The goal should be to make policy modestly restrictive so we can sustainably deliver both maximum employment and stable prices."
Logan is a voter this year on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee, though she will move into a nonvoting role in 2027.
"Markets bottom on bad news," is one of those smart-sounding rules of thumb that proves true just often enough to remain a Wall Street cliché in good standing.
Did the brutal weeks-long punishment of AI stocks culminate last week and reverse higher Monday after a pileup of adverse headlines? In the past week, American voters resoundingly opposed data-center construction across much of the country and Anthropic lowered its target IPO valuation just before a sex-and-espionage scandal struck the one-man embodiment of the entire AI economy, Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
The story of a market taking a cue from a crescendo of bad news after a nasty setback to stage a resounding bounce holds together well enough for now, after Monday's 3.4% jump in the Nasdaq-100 and 7% rip in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX), even as Nvidia shed 4.3%. Read more .
The three major averages began Tuesday's session under pressure.
The S&P 500 slipped 0.7% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 249 points, or 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite lost 0.9%.
The 10-year Treasury note yield rose on Tuesday after hotter-than-expected U.S. consumer price index data for October.
The benchmark yield was last up by more than 8 basis points to 4.95%.
The consumer price index rose by 0.4% month over month in October , reigniting inflation fears as traders brace for a potential Fed rate hike in December. Economists polled by Dow Jones expected an increase of 0.3%.
Check out CNBC's live blog to read more about the stocks making premarket moves here .
Falling gasoline prices provided some relief to consumers in October, but Federal Reserve officials are increasingly concerned that inflation pressures elsewhere in the economy are proving harder to contain.
Prices at the pump declined by more than 4%, according to the Energy Information Administration, providing a respite from a surge that had added more than a dollar a gallon over the past year.
However, the consumer price index for the month, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics will release Tuesday at 8:30 a.m., is expected to show only a slight let-up.
Read the full story here .
Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 to $78 per share, according to an updated filing on Tuesday, bringing the five-year-old artificial intelligence lab a step closer to a potentially historic Nasdaq debut.
At the high end of the range, Anthropic would net up to $64.35 billion in proceeds through the IPO. The company could end up being worth up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, up from the $965 billion valuation it announced as part of a funding round in May.
The Federal Reserve needs to follow through on an expected rate hike next month to maintain credibility, said Governor Christopher Waller , who also suggested a larger half-point increase may be warranted.

articles.title_orig: Goldman Sachs calls chip stocks 'oversold.' Here are the names it says to buy.
articles.title_zh: Goldman Sachs calls chip stocks 'oversold.' Here are the names it says to buy.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Goldman Sachs is sifting through the AI stock rubble in search of bargains.
"We believe stocks are now clearly in oversold territory," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said about semiconductor stocks.
Three of his top names to buy: Nvidia ( NVDA ), Broadcom ( AVGO ), and AMD ( AMD ).
"Even in a 'no growth' scenario for 2028 (which we see as relatively unlikely), NVDA/AVGO are trading 12X/13X this baseline — which we believe valuations are compelling at current levels," Schneider wrote in a note. "We find AMD to be very attractive given the growth we believe it can achieve, albeit at a less compelling valuation."
It has been a brutal run for tech stocks in November.
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) lost 4.3% of its market value on Nov. 5 as investors assessed what a blue wave on Election Day would mean for the build-out of AI data centers. The move wiped out $3 trillion in value.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) plunged 1,800 points in its worst single-day rout since 2020. The tech-heavy Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) cratered 5.5%, dragged down by semiconductor and cloud giants such as Micron ( MU ) and Sandisk ( SNDK ).
Stocks have continued to trade with a downward bias, especially semiconductor names.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is down 21% in the past month, and 6% in November alone.
"We believe the market has been contending with competing tensions relative to semiconductors: (1) How does the funding gap between current capex and free cash flows for hyperscalers and AI model labs levels get closed? (2) Is there sufficient land/power/shell coming on line to match current Street estimates for Semis?" Schneider explained. "Following the US elections on Nov. 3, the second of these tensions came into greater focus with greater uncertainty around the pace of datacenter builds in states such as Texas."
He added, "[Although] we recognize there may be few catalysts for stocks to move higher before year end, we think risk/reward is compelling for select names at current levels."

articles.title_orig: 10 PS Plus Extra, Premium Games for November 2026 Announced
articles.title_zh: 10 PS Plus Extra, Premium Games for November 2026 Announced
articles.content_orig:
Soul Reaver 2 and Freedom Wars  Remastered join PlayStation Plus Premium.
This month, embark on an inspiring mission of human connection in Death Stranding 2: On the Beach, assemble a one-of-a-kind crew as you explore the open sea in Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii, navigate the cult-controlled ruins, natural caves, and nuclear bunkers of a green and unpleasant British countryside in Atomfall, or explore a vast world map with an abundance of captivating locations in Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake. All these titles and more are available in November’s PlayStation Plus Game Catalog lineup*. Meanwhile, Soul Reaver 2 and Freedom Wars Remastered land into PlayStation Plus Premium. The full lineup will be available to play from November 17, unless otherwise noted.
Death Stranding 2: On the Beach | PS5
Embark on an inspiring mission of human connection beyond the UCA. Join Sam for the next chapter of his journey as he attempts to connect Australia to the Chiral Network. Navigate a living environment through day and night cycles, natural disasters including earthquakes, sandstorms and forest fires, and Timefall – a rain that instantly ages everything it touches. To traverse this dangerous landscape, you’ll need to build new types of infrastructure, master specialised equipment, and confront (or evade) the otherworldly creatures that roam the fractured world.
Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii | PS5, PS4
A new legend begins as you step into the steel toe boots of Goro Majima, a man who has lost his memory and reinvents himself as a pirate on the open sea. Embark on an over-the-top, modern-day pirate adventure with an ex-yakuza, now pirate captain and his crew as they engage in exhilarating combat on land and sea in the hunt for lost memories and a legendary treasure.
Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii will be available November 24 in the US, the UK and Japan.
A survival-action game inspired by real-life events, Atomfall is set five years after the Windscale nuclear disaster in Northern England. Explore the fictional quarantine zone, scavenge, craft, barter, fight and talk your way through a British countryside setting filled with bizarre characters, mysticism, cults, and rogue government agencies. From Rebellion, the studio behind Sniper Elite and Zombie Army, Atomfall will challenge you to solve the dark mystery of what really happened.
Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake | PS5
A stunning reimagining of the beloved RPG masterpiece and narrative beginning to The Erdrick Trilogy. Years ago, the great hero Ortega bid farewell to his wife and child as he set off on a quest to defeat the villainous Archfiend, Baramos. Ortega failed his quest, and Baramos still threatens the world. Now, on their 16th birthday, Ortega’s only child is summoned by the king of Aliahan and entrusted with a mission of the highest import: to take on Ortega’s quest, vanquish Baramos and save the world.
In Trepang2, you play as an escaped soldier who has no memories of their past life, but is infused with supernatural abilities. Revenge is on your mind, and you’ll stop at nothing to get what you want. Deliver devastating punches, sneak around in the shadows, wield explosive weapons, and give the bad guys a taste of their own medicine. Fight back, find the truth and face a threat even deadlier than yourself.
Trepang2 will be available November 24 in the US and the UK.
Experience the full intensity of the 2026 MotoGP Championship with all the official riders, teams, bikes and tracks in a more authentic way: for the first time, the real-world results dynamically update Riders Ratings, directly influencing in-game performance throughout the season. Step into the spotlight and track your journey with dazzling Collectible Cards celebrating your progress.
MotoGP 26 will be available November 24 in the US and the UK.
Join the ever-expanding experience of Hell Let Loose – a hardcore World War Two first person shooter with epic battles of 100 players with infantry, tanks, artillery, a dynamically shifting front line and a unique resource based RTS-inspired meta-game. Take to the battlefield in 50 vs 50 multiplayer across huge maps. Choose one of 14 playable roles within infantry, recon and armour unit types, each equipped with different weapons, vehicles and equipment. Play as an Officer, Scout, Machine Gunner, Medic, Engineer, Tank Commander and more to experience every aspect of World War II combat.
Hell Let Loose will be available tomorrow, November 11 in the US, the UK and November 12 in Japan.
Cricket 26 – The Official Game of the Ashes | PS5, PS4
Featuring the all-new Management Career, a bigger and better Pro Team, in-depth Ashes mode, and expanded control on and off the field from enhanced gameplay and in-depth strategies – Cricket 26 is The Ultimate Showdown.
Cricket 26 – The Official Game of the Ashes will be available November 24 in the US and the UK.
Soul Reaver 2 | PS5, PS4 In this sequel to the critically acclaimed Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver, reassume the role of Raziel, and battle back through the currents of time into pivotal, dangerous eras of Nosgoth’s past in your relentless pursuit of Kain. Encounter new enemies as you unearth the mysteries of Nosgoth’s ancient races, and expose the schemes that lie behind the corruption of the Pillars.
Freedom Wars Remastered | PS5, PS4
In a distant future where all resources on earth have been depleted, being alive is a sin by itself. Born into a one-million-year prison sentence, you must survive deadly missions to earn any hope of freedom. Die in prison or live on the battlefield. The choice is yours. Use your most trusted weapon, your Thorn, to dominate the battlefield. Stand alongside your allies and your warden cyborg Accessory to face off against powerful enemies.

articles.title_orig: Chinese Israel envoy rejects claims Beijing provides military assistance to Iran
articles.title_zh: Chinese Israel envoy rejects claims Beijing provides military assistance to Iran
articles.content_orig:
Shelves were left bare by the cyber-attacks
Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as "baseless and hostile".
On Monday, the French authorities blamed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for the string of hacks, which foreign minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot said were "unprecedented" in terms of their scale and "level of aggression".
He added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions.
The French cyber-attacks, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food, were followed by a similar hacks against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
On Monday, some Iranian media outlets denied the French accusations, but there had been no official comment until Tuesday's statement from Iran's foreign ministry.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of CoopÃ©rative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.
Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.

articles.title_orig: U.S. gas prices fall below $4 for the first time since July
articles.title_zh: U.S. gas prices fall below $4 for the first time since July
articles.content_orig:
Americans may finally find some relief at the pump.
The national average price of regular gasoline fell below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, reaching $3.9788 on Tuesday, according to AAA . Prices are down about 17 cents from a week ago and nearly 39 cents from a month ago.
The decline comes after energy inflation slowed significantly in October. Energy prices increased 0.7% during the month, a far cry from the 5.2% surge seen in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics . The BLS' gasoline index increased 1% over the month, after advancing 9.1% in September.
Bespoke Investment Group pointed out that gasoline prices also tend to decline at this time of the year, making part of the recent relief seasonal.
"While lower oil prices have been a tailwind for the relief at the pump, it's also perfectly normal for gas prices to be falling at this time of year, so if they weren't, there would really be something wrong," the firm said.
The drop at the pump followed a sharp retreat in crude oil. International oil benchmark Brent crude on Tuesday briefly fell below $90 a barrel for the first time since August as comments from U.S. President Donald Trump fueled hopes for an end to Washington's nearly nine-month conflict with Iran.
Recovering oil flows from the Persian Gulf have also eased supply concerns. Regional crude exports have returned to an estimated 80% to 85% of prewar levels, including pipeline shipments, according to ING .
"Energy markets remain under pressure as hopes for a de-escalation in the Middle East reduce geopolitical risk premiums. Oil extended its losses as Gulf supply flows continued to recover, while European gas also moved lower," analysts at ING wrote.
However, the Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller warned Tuesday that energy shocks may have more persistent effects on inflation than they did before the pandemic.
"While I am pleased to see energy prices down from their high rates over the past week or so, they are still quite elevated relative to the start of the year, and the ultimate effect on inflation will depend on what levels are sustained," he said.

articles.title_orig: iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on
articles.title_zh: iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on
articles.content_orig:
iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta , and it introduces a new iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.
I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.
But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.
For example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.
I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a new optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.
Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if you have ‘Windowed Apps’ enabled you’ll see a new option below it: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom’
If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this new setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.
When the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.
I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The new setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.
Will you enable this new iPadOS 27.3 setting? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Scion Is Back, and It’s Bringing a Right-Hand Drive 3-Cylinder Kei Truck to the U.S. Market
articles.title_zh: Scion Is Back, and It’s Bringing a Right-Hand Drive 3-Cylinder Kei Truck to the U.S. Market
articles.content_orig:
Scion lived a short life, the victim of bad financial timing and millennial misunderstandings. But its parent company, Toyota, is about to give the brand another go—and its market research appears to be spot-on this time, as the Japanese automaker announces a new three-cylinder Kei truck for the U.S. market .
Officially known as the Scion Kei-01, the new model takes traditional Japanese compactness and adds North American levels of capability. The heart of the Kei-01 is a 660cc three-cylinder engine paired with a continuously variable transmission and proper four-wheel drive with push-button lock-up. At 11 feet long and five feet wide, the Kei truck will be even smaller than a modern Mini Cooper.
The Kei-01 will be right-hand-drive, have a maximum speed of 25 miles per hour, and is intended to comply with federal safety requirements for low-speed vehicles. An easily accessible three-way fold-down cargo bed, a payload capacity of 600 pounds, and an extended cabin design with a raised roofline were included specifically for the North American market. Scion has not revealed power figures for the Kei-01, but Toyota did confirm the Kei truck will be available in the U.S. market.
Initially, the Kei-01 will arrive in the U.S. as part of a fleet vehicle pilot program. Scion said this new Kei truck will be an intentionally low-volume, niche vehicle for specific kinds of fleets; it’s targeting small business owners looking for an affordable urban commercial vehicle, farmers requiring a dependable daily workhorse, and municipalities, universities, and corporate campuses seeking efficient fleet vehicles. Last-mile delivery services and outdoor enthusiasts are also being targeted by Toyota. Fleet sales will route through select Toyota dealerships, and the truck will be produced at Toyota Motor Manufacturing Indiana in the second half of 2027.
However, Toyota says it is open to expanding availability of the bite-sized pickup. “Based on market conditions, customer demand, and operational considerations, Toyota may consider expanding availability to limited retail sales at a later date. Additional information and the broader sales strategy will be shared as plans are finalized,” the carmaker stated.
Two additional Scion concept vehicles were showcased alongside the Kei-01 at Toyota Motor North America events in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan, and Frisco, Texas, on Tuesday, November 10. The Scion SxS Concept takes on off-roading with a side-by-side frame and a high-output turbocharged four-cylinder hybrid powertrain. The off-road-focused model will feature over 300 horsepower, significant suspension articulation, and a nimble footprint; there will even be a Silent Mode that shifts motive power to the electric drivetrain.
Additionally, Scion is showing off the BKE Concept, a new kind of mobility tool for the revived automotive brand. Packing only two wheels, the BKE Concept is a personal mobility scooter made for the great outdoors. Scion didn’t provide any other details about the BKE Concept, but it appears to be a comfortable urban commuter.
Regardless of the ultimate plans of Scion’s new Kei truck and concept vehicles, the return of the fun-loving brand is worth celebrating. Toyota has been razor-focused on car enthusiasts with its Gazoo Racing and off-road-focused models, and Scion offers another opportunity for enthusiast appeal. But instead of focusing on young buyers exclusively, Scion will be a “freedom lab” for Toyota, with a focus on experimentation.
“The future of mobility will not be defined by one vehicle, one technology or one way of thinking,” said Simon Humphries, chief branding officer, head of design, Toyota Motor Corporation. “Scion by Toyota gives us a place to challenge conventional thinking, explore new possibilities and create mobility in new ways. The KEI-01, SxS, and BKE concepts each represent a different possibility—and together, they show what can happen when curiosity leads the way.”
A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

articles.title_orig: Google releases Gemini 4 Carbon with agent ‘swarm’ feature
articles.title_zh: Google releases Gemini 4 Carbon with agent ‘swarm’ feature
articles.content_orig:
It ‘pushes the frontier even further’ than its last release, Argon.﻿
It ‘pushes the frontier even further’ than its last release, Argon.﻿
Google is rolling out its latest AI model, Gemini 4 Carbon, to the general public after releasing it to a select group of “cybersecurity defenders” two weeks ago. Google claims Carbon is its “strongest model” yet, and capable of competing with the very best systems from Anthropic and OpenAI.
Google says Gemini 4 Carbon “pushes the frontier even further” than Argon, referring to the company’s other frontier model that launched only last month . The company said Argon will likely remain “the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work,” but that Carbon is “built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence,” such as complex, multi-step coding and open-ended scientific research.
To highlight Carbon’s utility for long-horizon work involving AI agents, Google said it is also previewing a “swarm” feature on its agentic development platform Antigravity, which will let users turn a single prompt “into a coordinated team of agents.”
Carbon is rolling out today via the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, Google said in a blog post. It will also be available to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app, the AI Mode in Search, and on Antigravity. It is not clear when — or if — Carbon will be available to lower tier subscribers or free users.
As with the launch of Argon, Google is pricing Carbon very competitively. The model is launching with an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, around a fifth the cost of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and a quarter the cost of Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model, which launched yesterday . Even after those costs double at the end November — when the introductory period of lower prices finishes — Carbon will still be significantly cheaper than frontier rivals on a per-token basis, though this doesn’t necessarily translate to lower costs as models can use different numbers of tokens for the same tasks.
Benchmarks cited by Google when it first announced Carbon suggest the model is one of the most powerful on the market across most metrics, behind Fable 5.2. It should be noted that companies can and do cherry-pick benchmark results to show their tools in the best possible light.
The release, hot on the heels of Argon, marks a decisive return for Google at the very forefront of AI research . For months, frontier development looked like a two-horse race between Anthropic and OpenAI.

articles.title_orig: Oil Prices Have Tumbled in November. Here’s Why.
articles.title_zh: Oil Prices Have Tumbled in November. Here’s Why.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
NEW YORK, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Oil prices slid about 2% to fresh two-month lows on Tuesday after US officials downplayed the need for additional military action against Iran, easing fears of additional Middle East supply disruptions.
Brent futures fell $1.93, or 2.1%, to $90.64 a barrel at 10:28 a.m. ‌ET (1528 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell $1.44, or 1.7%, to $85.41.
That put both crude benchmarks on track for their lowest closes since August 28. On ‌Monday, both contracts closed at their lowest since August 31.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that he told Group of Seven allies that the US economic sanctions and naval blockade are working so ​well that US President Donald Trump does not need to conduct major combat operations in Iran.
Rubio made the comments during a meeting in Paris of foreign ministers from the G7, which comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, as well as the European Union.
On Monday, Trump said he plans to hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the time being after appeals from countries in the region, including from Qatar's prime minister in White House talks.
"The market continues to prioritize President Trump's more conciliatory tone toward ‌Iran since the midterms," said Tim Waterer, chief market ⁠analyst at KCM Trade.
In last week's US midterm elections, voters focused on the rising cost of living, which was fueled by Republican Trump's trade tariffs and higher energy costs from the war with Iran, and handed solid majorities in both houses of Congress to the ⁠Democratic Party.
Trump, in a Reuters interview and a later appearance in the White House press briefing room, said he plans to keep up a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz for now. Before the US and Israel started attacking Iran in February, about 20% of the world's oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
More than eight months into the conflict, ​Trump ​has played down the likelihood of major warfare restarting soon but remains unwilling to accept an ​existing Iranian truce plan. Senior US and Gulf officials have cast ‌doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.
Mutual attacks continue, with the US striking Iran's Qeshm island overnight, according to Iranian state media, and Iran attacking tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz this month while its Yemeni Houthi allies have hit Saudi Arabia.
Russian and Ukrainian officials met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their first peace talks since February as Trump's envoys launched a new push to end the war in Ukraine.
The US-brokered meeting followed US contacts with both sides in recent weeks, which Trump's representative Jared Kushner said had narrowed the gaps between their positions.
Rubio described the meeting as very productive, without giving details.
Despite US optimism, the warring sides remain far ‌apart on terms for a possible settlement, more than 4-1/2 years after Russia's full-scale invasion ​of Ukraine. Russia controls about a fifth of its neighbor's territory.
Russia was the world's third-biggest crude oil ​producer behind the US and Saudi Arabia in 2025, US energy data showed. ​Sanctions designed to keep Russian energy out of global markets after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine have helped support oil prices.
Any deal to ‌end Russia's invasion of Ukraine could allow Russia to export more.
In a move that could reduce future ​oil demand, investors said the release of data on Tuesday showing US consumer prices increased by more than expected in October made it more likely the US Federal Reserve would raise interest rates half a percentage point at its December meeting.
A strong jobs market, resilient economic growth and inflation stuck above the Fed's ​2% target for nearly six years all suggest further tightening ‌is required.
Central banks, like the Fed, use interest rates to control inflation. Higher interest rates raise consumer costs, which can reduce economic growth and ​demand for oil.
(Reporting by Scott DiSavino in New York and Enes Tunagur in London; Additional Reporting by Seher Dareen in London, Sethuraman N R ​in New Delhi and Noel John in BengaluruEditing by David Goodman and Nia Williams)

articles.title_orig: Meta’s AI agent Muse lands on Apple Watch and Android Wear OS
articles.title_zh: Meta’s AI agent Muse lands on Apple Watch and Android Wear OS
articles.content_orig:
Meta is bringing its Muse AI agent to the Apple Watch and Android’s Wear OS, the company announced on Monday. With the launch, users can now interact with Meta’s AI assistant through voice calls, text messages, or dictation directly on their smartwatch.
Works around the clock, and now on your wrist. Muse is now on Apple Watch and Wear OS ⌚️ pic.twitter.com/97QRap5XKz
The smartwatch launch comes just a month after Meta introduced a dedicated iPad app for Muse. First launched on the App Store in September, the AI assistant’s expansion across Apple devices signals Meta’s growing ambitions for its consumer AI product and its focus on making Muse a central part of its ecosystem.
Muse is now one of dozens of consumer-facing AI agents competing for users’ attention. Like many of its competitors, it allows users to connect their accounts to manage email, meetings, bills, and more, while also handling tasks such as booking reservations, ordering groceries, setting goals, and making purchases.
Users can also personalize their Muse avatar to their liking and change it into something that resembles a person, an animal, or another type of character.
Despite being a relatively new product, Meta has wasted little time introducing new capabilities to Muse.
A few days ago, Meta launched Spaces , a new way to communicate and collaborate with Muse. Spaces function as dedicated conversations around specific topics, which Meta describes as “custom experiences” as they’re mini apps that are built on the fly. They appear in the sidebar of the Muse interface and bring up a focused conversation where the AI agent works toward a particular goal on the user’s behalf.
Last week, Meta rolled out the ability for users in the U.S. to video chat with their Muse AI avatar. Meta said Muse will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that reflect the tone and context of the conversation as it speaks. It’s worth noting that Muse doesn’t actually see users, but can hear them and respond in real time.
Shortly after its launch, Muse became one of just 12 mobile apps to have surpassed 10 million U.S. downloads within their first 40 days in the App Store. Only 11 other apps have achieved this milestone, with Meta’s Threads being the most recent in July 2023.

articles.title_orig: Board of Peace says Israel's aid response after Gaza floods 'insufficent'
articles.title_zh: Board of Peace says Israel's aid response after Gaza floods 'insufficent'
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has called on Israel to immediately allow all necessary humanitarian supplies into Gaza after rain flooded tens of thousands of tents.
The US-backed body, established to oversee the implementation of Trump's Gaza peace plan, acknowledged the steps now being considered by Israel, but said "the response remains insufficient".
Israel's military agency in charge of co-ordinating aid into Gaza said it had allowed in tens of thousands of tents and trucks with winter supplies, but added reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".
On Sunday, three children and a woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in the central Strip.
Most people in Gaza have been displaced because of Israel's military actions. Around 65% of the population, about 1.4 million people, now live in tents or makeshift shelters, the UN says.
Standing soaked in Gaza City, Mohammed Jneid told the AFP news agency that heavy rains hit from one side and sewage overflowed on them from the other, with the ground and tents no longer able to hold.
"We have nothing left, no bedding, no food, nothing," he said.
Sitting inside her tent, Islam Al Mobayed told AFP there were seven children there, five of them young.
"This is not life," she said. "We are exhausted, we are tired of this entire life."
In rare criticism of Israel, the Board of Peace said it had been urging the Israeli government to authorise the entry of essential goods for temporary shelter and water and sanitation infrastructure.
The Board added that delays in approving the entry of supplies "exacerbated the consequences of a foreseeable humanitarian challenge" and delayed the start of decommissioning weapons and transferring Hamas authority to a transitional government.
It also said Hamas's failure to disarm and transfer power had compounded the difficulties facing Gaza's civilians.
The UN's humanitarian agency OCHA said more than 150,000 tents were outside Gaza ready to go in, but aid efforts were constrained "by Israeli restrictions on the entry of supplies and equipment and funding shortfalls".
UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov said on Monday that stocks of essential shelter and winter items inside Gaza had been exhausted.
"Israeli authorities must immediately lift all restrictions on entry of the supplies," he said, adding "we have run out of time".
Israel's foreign ministry spokeswoman Michal Maayan on Monday said Israel had in recent months put in place a winter plan in coordination with the Board of Peace and international charities.
That plan has brought in more than 91,000 tents and 8,200-plus trucks with tarpaulins, blankets, winter clothing, and other equipment, according to Cogat, the Israeli military body responsible for aid.
Cogat said it would not allow in equipment that could be used for military purposes.
Maayon accused Hamas of hoarding aid, saying: "Hamas is responsible for the delays in making more progress in the Strip, and winter-related hardships are a consequence of Hamas's action and policy."
In response to the Board of Peace, Hamas said in a statement published on Palestinian media that its comment "presents a distorted account of the causes of the disaster". The group denied it was responsible for ceasefire delays, pointing to a statement in August from Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators that accused Israel of violations.
Hamas said Israeli restrictions prevent the entry of materials necessary for shelter and recovery - and added the Board as the ceasefire implementor should look at its own "serious shortcoming".
Under the deal to end the two-year-long war in October 2025, Hamas agreed to give up governance and its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the 60% of Gaza it still occupied. Israel, however, has insisted Hamas must fully disarm before withdrawal.
The dispute has left the next stages of the peace plan stalled, with both sides blaming each other.
The war in Gaza began after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 when around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.
The Israeli military campaign in response has killed 74,645 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable. More than 1,600 people have been killed since the ceasefire in October last year.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza since then.

Samsung is working on a long overdue redesign for its Galaxy S27 series and, this week, we’re getting a fresh look.
We’ve already seen it in renders, but leaker Sonny Dickson took to Twitter/X today to present an image of Galaxy S27 Pro, Ultra, and S27+ dummy units, and it tells us a few things.
First, we get to see the redesign again, this time in “real life.” That’s, of course, with the caveat that these aren’t real devices, and probably aren’t reflective of the final design either. The Pro and Ultra both have a full-width camera island akin to Apple’s latest iPhone design language, and a big departure from the vertical camera array that Samsung insisted was its “core identity” mere months ago.
Importantly, we can also see the size difference between Galaxy S27 Ultra and S27 Pro, with the Pro being noticeably smaller compared to both the Ultra and the S27+. For small(er) phone fans, it’s looking great .
All of that said, adding a bit of controversy to this image is leaker Ice Universe, who says “this picture is wrong.”
Ice points out that the Galaxy S27 Ultra and Pro both do not have a fourth camera lens, which is correct based on recent leaks . That said, it’s not much of a leap to assume these dummy units are based on an older design, or are confusing a sensor. After all, these are mainly used to test accessories and, this early on, there’s plenty of room for inaccuracy.

articles.title_orig: Changes are coming to Social Security in January — here’s what Americans should know
articles.title_zh: Changes are coming to Social Security in January — here’s what Americans should know
articles.content_orig:
Starting in January, Social Security recipients will see two major changes.
The Social Security Administration (SSA) — a program providing financial benefits to eligible workers after reaching retirement age — will increase benefits and taxes. Back in October, the SSA announced that recipients will see a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) .
The COLA is the yearly increase meant to help Social Security keep up with rising prices.
This means nearly 72 million retirees will most likely see their Social Security benefits increase by about $75 per month starting in January. The increased payments will hit roughly 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) beginning on December 31, 2026.
Another change to hit millions of beneficiaries — some added taxes. Based on increases in average wages, the maximum amount of income subject to Social Security will increase next year.
For example, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax — known as taxable maximum — is set to increase from $184,500 to $192,300 in 2027.
The move will impact higher earners, as many will soon start paying Social Security taxes on an additional $7,800 in reported income. For example, someone earning at least $192,300 would likely pay up to $483.60 more annually in Social Security taxes.
The agency has recently announced another revision — the biggest change in its 91-year history . The SSA revealed it has officially “cleaned up” the comprehensive Social Security Number (SSN) database.
SSA records are referenced by federal government agencies and in states to validate identities — which helps prevent improper payments of taxpayer dollars. While it may seem like a small, administrative change, the move safeguards identity data, helps to prevent fraud and preserves proper program administration.
According to the office, it added 17 million dates of death to records that previously lacked this information, updated about 25 million records that previously had missing citizenship information and more.
For most recipients, it’s business as usual. No Social Security numbers have been taken; your monthly checks are still coming and recipients will still see a COLA bump.
To view your COLA notice online, head to your Social Security account. If you receive paperless notices, you may view and save your COLA notice in the “Message Center” starting in late November.
However, you must create an online “my Social Security account” and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see yours online. The agency will send paper notices with updated benefit amounts in early December.
And don’t forget — you may see an early Social Security check as Veterans Day falls on a Wednesday.
